nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; memoirist, novelist and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: Chinese American memoirist and novelist, whose The Woman Warrior changed the American memoir by refusing to choose between the life and the legend, and whose China Men and Tripmaster Monkey extended that refusal across two further books
biography: Maxine Hong Kingston was born Maxine Ting Ting Hong in Stockton, California, on 27 October 1940, the daughter of Chinese immigrants who had run a laundry and later a gambling house; she grew up listening to her mother's 'talk-stories', which became the method of her writing. She took a BA in English at the University of California at Berkeley in 1962 and a teaching certificate in 1963, married the actor Earll Kingston in 1962, and taught English and mathematics in California and then in Hawaii, where she moved in 1967. The Woman Warrior: Memoirs of a Girlhood Among Ghosts (1976) won the National Book Critics Circle Award for general nonfiction and made her - in disputes with Frank Chin that are now a standard part of the discussion of Asian American literature - the most controversial and most read Chinese American writer of the period. China Men (1980) won the National Book Award for nonfiction; Tripmaster Monkey: His Fake Book (1989) was her first novel; Hawai'i One Summer (1987), To Be the Poet (2002), The Fifth Book of Peace (2003) and I Love a Broad Margin to My Life (2011) followed. She taught at Berkeley from 1990, was arrested twice in anti-war protests, received the National Humanities Medal in 1997 and the National Medal of Arts in 2013, and is the subject of the documentary Maxine Hong Kingston: Talking Story (2010).
literary_profile: Books: The Woman Warrior (1976), China Men (1980), Hawai'i One Summer (1987), Through the Black Curtain (1987), Tripmaster Monkey: His Fake Book (1989), To Be the Poet (2002), The Fifth Book of Peace (2003) and I Love a Broad Margin to My Life (2011).
stylistic_characteristics: A first-person 'I' that is never quite the author; the 'talk-story' as the structural unit, so that a chapter begins as a folktale and ends as a memory; direct address to the reader and to the dead; a syntax that keeps the cadence of spoken Chinese-influenced English; and a refusal to tell the reader which parts are true.
intellectual_concerns: The relation of a daughter to a mother whose stories are her history; Chinese and Chinese American traditions, and the cost of leaving them; silence, and the voice a girl has to find; immigration, the paper sons and the exclusion laws; and the fictionality of all autobiography.
historical_significance: The Woman Warrior is the book that made the Asian American memoir a national form and one of the most widely taught American books of the period. Its National Book Critics Circle Award, the decade of argument it provoked about authenticity and representation, and its influence on the memoirs and novels of the 1980s and 1990s make it a founding text of Asian American literature; Kingston's two national medals confirm her standing.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Kingston and from the copyright page of The Woman Warrior, which gives 'No Name Woman' as having appeared in slightly different form in Viva, January 1975; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records the book once for both of its Norton selections - 'No Name Woman' and the excerpt from 'A Song for a Barbarian Reed Pipe' - so China Men, Tripmaster Monkey and the later books have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; Laguna Pueblo novelist, poet and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: Laguna Pueblo novelist, poet and essayist, whose Ceremony is the central novel of the Native American Renaissance and whose Storyteller made the photograph, the poem and the oral account parts of a single form
biography: Leslie Marmon Silko was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico, on 5 March 1948 and grew up at Laguna Pueblo, where her family - Laguna, Mexican and white - had lived for generations; she has said that she grew up 'on the border' of the Pueblo and never fully belonged to any of its parts, an experience that shapes everything she wrote. She took a BA in English at the University of New Mexico in 1969 and attended law school for three years before turning to writing. Laguna Woman (1974) was her first book of poems; Ceremony (1977), her first novel, tells the story of a Laguna veteran of the Second World War who is healed by a Navajo ceremony and a traditional story, and it is generally regarded as the finest novel of the Native American Renaissance. Storyteller (1981) combined poems, photographs and prose in a form modelled on the Pueblo oral tradition; Almanac of the Dead (1991), a vast novel of the Americas across five centuries, and Gardens in the Dunes (1999) followed, with the essays of Yellow Woman and a Beauty of the Spirit (1996) and Conversations with Leslie Marmon Silko (2000). She has received a MacArthur Fellowship (1981), the Native Writers' Circle of the Americas Lifetime Achievement Award and the 2020 lifetime achievement award of the Academy of American Poets.
literary_profile: Fiction: Ceremony (1977), Almanac of the Dead (1991) and Gardens in the Dunes (1999). Poetry: Laguna Woman (1974). Mixed form: Storyteller (1981). Nonfiction and essays: Yellow Woman and a Beauty of the Spirit (1996) and Conversations with Leslie Marmon Silko (2000).
stylistic_characteristics: A narrative that moves between the present and the mythic without marking the transition; the Pueblo oral tradition used as a structural principle rather than as decoration; a prose that is plain and declarative in the modern sections and incantatory in the traditional ones; the landscape of the Southwest presented as inhabited rather than as scenery; and an ending that returns to the story that opened the book.
intellectual_concerns: The survival of Native people and Native stories under colonisation; healing, and the difference between curing a body and restoring a person; the Second World War and the reservation; the land as a living relation rather than property; the oral tradition as history; and the continuity of women's knowledge across generations.
historical_significance: Silko is one of the two or three central figures of the Native American Renaissance and the writer whose Ceremony is most often named as its finest novel. Storyteller changed what a book of Native American writing could look like, Almanac of the Dead is a landmark of the 1990s novel, and her MacArthur Fellowship of 1981 makes her one of the first Native American writers so honoured.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Silko and from the bibliographic records of Laguna Woman and Storyteller; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records two Norton selections - 'Lullaby' and 'Language and Literature from a Pueblo Indian Perspective' - separately, since they belong to different books, so the novels and the later essays have no records and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist, poet, essayist, editor and songwriter writing in English
literary_identity: American novelist, poet and editor, the founder of the Neo-HooDoo aesthetic, whose The Free-Lance Pallbearers, Mumbo Jumbo and the Yardbird anthologies made a satirical, syncretic Black American postmodernism that has been an alternative to the realist novel for fifty years
biography: Ishmael Scott Reed was born in Chattanooga, Tennessee, on 22 February 1938 and grew up in Buffalo, New York, where his mother worked as a housekeeper and his stepfather in a steel mill. He took a degree in English at the University of Buffalo in 1960, worked as a journalist and a radio announcer, moved to New York in 1962, co-founded the East Village Other - one of the first underground papers - and became a central figure in the Black Arts Movement, though never a believer in any of its orthodoxies. The Free-Lance Pallbearers (1967) was his first novel; Yellow Back Radio Broke-Down (1969) and Mumbo Jumbo (1972) followed, the last a comic history of the Harlem Renaissance as a conflict between Neo-HooDoo and the Western aesthetic, and now a standard text of the American postmodern novel. Conjure (1972) collected his poems; he edited the Yardbird anthologies (1973-1977) and later the multi-volume Before Columbus Foundation anthologies, founded the Before Columbus Foundation and its American Book Awards in 1976, and published Flight to Canada (1976), The Terrible Twos (1982), Reckless Eyeballing (1986), The Terrible Threes (1989), Japanese by Spring (1993) and Juice! (2011), as well as six further books of poems and collections of essays.
literary_profile: Novels: The Free-Lance Pallbearers (1967), Yellow Back Radio Broke-Down (1969), Mumbo Jumbo (1972), The Last Days of Louisiana Red (1974), Flight to Canada (1976), The Terrible Twos (1982), Reckless Eyeballing (1986), The Terrible Threes (1989), Japanese by Spring (1993) and Juice! (2011). Poetry: catechism of d neoamerican hoodoo church (1970), Conjure (1972), Chattanooga (1973), A Secretary to the Spirits (1978), New and Collected Poems (1988) and others. Anthologies and essays: 19 Necromancers from Now (1970), the Yardbird series (1973-1977), Shrovetide in Old New Orleans (1978), God Made Alaska, He Just Didn't Finish It (1982) and Airing Dirty Laundry (1993).
stylistic_characteristics: A satirical prose built on collage, parody and pastiche; chapters that switch register and medium; hoodoo as a principle of composition as well as a subject; the detective and the western used as found forms to be broken; and a narrator who is openly partisan and openly funny.
intellectual_concerns: The conflict between African-derived and European aesthetics in American culture; the suppression of Black cultural history and its underground survival; satire as a political instrument; the publishing industry and the politics of who gets anthologised; and American myth as a source to be plundered rather than revered.
historical_significance: Reed is the founder of the Neo-HooDoo aesthetic and one of the most consistently inventive American novelists of the last half-century. Mumbo Jumbo is a set text in courses on the American postmodern novel, the Yardbird anthologies changed the visibility of Black writers in the 1970s, and his American Book Awards remain an alternative to the established prizes; his influence is acknowledged by writers as different as Toni Morrison and Paul Beatty.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Reed and from catalogue records of Conjure; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - 'Neo-HooDoo Manifesto' - which belongs to Conjure (University of Massachusetts Press, 1972), so the ten novels, the other books of poems and the anthologies have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; essayist and memoirist writing in English
literary_identity: Mexican American essayist whose Hunger of Memory made the memoir of assimilation a national controversy and whose prose has been a sustained argument against the politics of affirmative action and bilingual education
biography: Richard Rodriguez was born in San Francisco on 31 July 1944, the son of Mexican immigrant parents from the state of Jalisco; the family moved to Sacramento when he was a small child, and his first language was Spanish until the nuns at his Catholic school asked his parents to speak English at home - an episode that became the founding scene of Hunger of Memory. He took a BA in English at Stanford in 1967, an MA at Columbia in 1969, and studied for a PhD in English at Berkeley, which he abandoned after three years; he was, by his own account, a beneficiary of affirmative action and has been its most articulate critic. Hunger of Memory: The Education of Richard Rodriguez (1982) made him famous and controversial in equal measure, particularly among Mexican American writers who took its rejection of 'minority' identity as a betrayal. Days of Obligation: An Argument with My Mexican Father (1992) and Brown: The Last Discovery of America (2002) completed a trilogy on American race and class, and Darling: A Spiritual Autobiography (2013) followed. He has been an editor at the Pacific News Service, a correspondent for The NewsHour with Jim Lehrer on PBS, and a contributor to Harper's, The American Scholar and The New York Times.
literary_profile: Books: Hunger of Memory: The Education of Richard Rodriguez (1982), Days of Obligation: An Argument with My Mexican Father (1992), Brown: The Last Discovery of America (2002) and Darling: A Spiritual Autobiography (2013). Essays in Harper's, The American Scholar, The New York Times and elsewhere, and broadcast work for PBS.
stylistic_characteristics: A formal, essayistic English that is deliberately more literary than conversational; the first person used as an argument rather than a confession; the long periodic sentence; quotation and anecdote used as evidence; and a habit of refusing the conclusion the reader has been led to expect.
intellectual_concerns: Assimilation and its costs; language and the loss of a mother tongue; class and the American university; race and the argument over affirmative action; the Mexican American family; and, in the later books, the religious imagination and the body.
historical_significance: Hunger of Memory is one of the most widely taught American memoirs of the period and the book that made assimilation into a public argument for a Mexican American writer. Its reception - praised as a classic of immigrant autobiography and attacked as a rejection of its own community - is a standing case in the discussion of American multiculturalism, and the trilogy it belongs to is central to the literature of American race.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Rodriguez and from the publication records of Hunger of Memory; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - the excerpt from Hunger of Memory - so the three later books and the uncollected essays have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

birthplace: Huddersfield, West Riding of Yorkshire, England
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet, playwright, novelist and translator writing in English
literary_identity: English poet of the West Yorkshire Pennines whose plain, wry, often violent narratives in contemporary speech made him the most widely read British poet of his generation, and the Poet Laureate since 2019
biography: Simon Robert Armitage was born in Huddersfield on 26 May 1963 and grew up in the village of Marsden, on the edge of the Pennines, where his family still lived and where most of his poems are set; his father wrote pantomimes for a local all-male troupe. He read geography at Portsmouth Polytechnic and took a master's degree in social work at the University of Manchester, and worked for several years as a probation officer, an experience that later underpins poems such as 'Remains' and the television work he did with soldiers. Zoom! (Bloodaxe, 1989) was his first collection; Kid (1992) won the Forward Prize for Best First Collection's successor, Book of Matches (1993) and The Dead Sea Poems (1995) established him, and Cloudcuckooland (1997) was shortlisted for the Whitbread Prize. The millennium poem Killing Time, broadcast and printed in 1999, made him a public figure, and the sequence of prose poems in Seeing Stars (2010) and the translations of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (2007), the Alliterative Morte Arthure (2012) and Pearl (2016) extended his range. He was Professor of Poetry at Oxford from 2015 to 2019, has been Professor of Poetry at Leeds since 2017, and was appointed Poet Laureate on 10 May 2019; he was awarded the CBE in 2010 and the Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry in 2018. His prose includes All Points North (1998), the Pennine Way account Walking Home (2012) and its sequel Walking Away, and the novels Little Green Man (2001) and The White Stuff (2004).
literary_profile: Collections: Zoom! (1989), Kid (1992), Book of Matches (1993), The Dead Sea Poems (1995), Cloudcuckooland (1997), Killing Time (1999), Selected Poems (2001), The Universal Home Doctor (2002), Travelling Songs (2002), The Shout: Selected Poems (2005), Tyrannosaurus Rex Versus the Corduroy Kid (2006), Seeing Stars (2010), The Death of King Arthur (2012), Paper Aeroplane: Selected Poems 1989-2014 (2014), The Unaccompanied (2017), Sandettie Light Vessel Automatic (2019), Magnetic Field: The Marsden Poems (2020) and Blossomise (2024). Translations: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (2007), The Alliterative Morte Arthure (2012), Pearl (2016), The Odyssey (2016). Prose: All Points North (1998), Walking Home (2012), Walking Away (2015). Novels: Little Green Man (2001), The White Stuff (2004).
stylistic_characteristics: A conversational, usually first-person line that sounds like speech but is metrically exact; short sentences; a Yorkshire vocabulary kept without ornament; sudden shifts of register from the demotic to the literary; narrative poems that withhold their moral; and endings that turn on a plain statement or a single image rather than a summary.
intellectual_concerns: Adolescence and the remembered places of a northern childhood; class, work and the probation service; the borderland between town and moor; violence, often casual and domestic; the body and its failures; the First World War and its commemorations; and, in the later work, the environment and the public poem.
historical_significance: Armitage is the most widely taught British poet of his generation and, since 2019, the official one. The directness of his line made him the standard counter-example to the difficulty of the modernist and Language poets, and his public standing - the millennium poem, the laureateship, the translations - has made him a test case for what a laureate can do. His poems are on the English school syllabus and the Norton Anthology of English Literature prints four of them, of which one, 'The Tyre', falls inside the period.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Armitage, checked against the Faber, Poetry Foundation and University of Leeds author pages; they were not checked against a printed bibliography, and the poems produced for projects, commissions and the Stanza Stones trail are not all gathered here. Installment 10 records one selection, 'The Tyre' - the only Armitage poem in the anthology first published 1946-2000, since 'Horses, M62' (2006), 'The English Astronaut' (2010) and 'Beck' (2019) are all after it - so the other collections, translations, novels and prose books have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, performer, children's writer and teacher writing in English and Spanish
literary_identity: Chicano poet, performer and activist, the first Latino Poet Laureate of the United States, whose bilingual, typographically restless poems make migration, the border and the campesino childhood of the San Joaquin Valley into a public American poetry
biography: Juan Felipe Herrera was born in Fowler, California, on 27 December 1948, the son of migrant farmworkers from Mexico, and spent his childhood in trailers and tents along the roads of the San Joaquin Valley; he has said that he attended more than forty schools. He took a B.A. in social anthropology at UCLA in 1972, an M.A. in the same subject at Stanford in 1980, and an MFA from the Iowa Writers' Workshop in 1990, and was involved in the Chicano civil rights movement and in experimental theatre in San Francisco in the 1970s. His first books came from small presses - Rebozos of Love (1974), Exiles of Desire (1983), Facegames (1987) and Akrilica (1989) - and he went on to publish more than thirty, including Border-Crosser with a Lamborghini Dream (1999), Notebooks of a Chile Verde Smuggler (2002), 187 Reasons Mexicanos Can't Cross the Border (2007), Half of the World in Light: New and Selected Poems (2008), which won the National Book Critics Circle Award, Senegal Taxi (2013), Notes on the Assemblage (2015), Every Day We Get More Illegal (2020) and the young-adult prose books and picture books for which he is also known. He taught at California State University, Fresno and held the Tomas Rivera Endowed Chair at UC Riverside until his retirement in 2015; he was Poet Laureate of California from 2012 to 2014 and the 21st Poet Laureate of the United States from 2015 to 2017, the first Latino to hold the office.
literary_profile: Poetry: Rebozos of Love (1974), Exiles of Desire (1983; reissued by Arte Publico Press, 1985), Facegames (1987), Akrilica (1989), Night Train to Tuxtla (1994), Border-Crosser with a Lamborghini Dream (1999), Loteria Cards and Fortune Poems (1999), Giraffe on Fire (2001), Notebooks of a Chile Verde Smuggler (2002), 187 Reasons Mexicanos Can't Cross the Border (2007), Half of the World in Light: New and Selected Poems (2008), Senegal Taxi (2013), Notes on the Assemblage (2015) and Every Day We Get More Illegal (2020). Prose and books for younger readers: Calling the Doves (1995), The Upside Down Boy (2000), Mayan Drifter (1997), Cinnamon Girl (2005), SkateFate (2011) and Jabberwalking (2018).
stylistic_characteristics: Code-switching between English and Spanish without translation or apology; long incantatory lines of accumulation and list; typographical experiment, including drawings and lettering, carried over from his work as a performance poet; the prose poem and the documentary fragment; and a public, declamatory register that is equally at home in the classroom and the protest.
intellectual_concerns: Migration, the border and the undocumented; the Mexican and Chicano past, from the pyramids to the farmworkers' strikes; the family, and especially the mother's voice; political violence and the disappeared; language itself, as a possession that is taken away and reclaimed; and, in the late work, the poet's public office and the dead of the present.
historical_significance: Herrera's laureateship in 2015 was the first for a Latino poet and made a bilingual, small-press, performance-trained writer the public face of American poetry; Half of the World in Light won the National Book Critics Circle Award and he received the Ruth Lilly Poetry Prize in 2022. Within the Norton Anthology of American Literature he is one of the Chicano writers - with Anzaldua and Cisneros - by whom the postwar canon admits Spanish-language American poetry, and two of the five poems printed there, 'Exiles' and 'Literary Asylums', date from his first collection and fall inside the period.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Herrera, the Library of Congress and Encyclopaedia Britannica author pages and Francisco A. Lomeli's Gilder Lehrman essay, which carries a bibliography of the collections; they were not checked against a printed bibliography, and the many small-press chapbooks of the 1970s and 1980s are not all gathered here. Installment 10 records two selections, 'Exiles' and 'Literary Asylums', both from Exiles of Desire (1983); the other three poems the anthology prints ('Half-Mexican', 'Borderbus' and the choke-hold poem) are after 2000 and are outside the period, so the later collections have no records and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; singer-songwriter and poet writing in English
literary_identity: American songwriter who carried the literary ambitions of the folk revival into rock and made the song lyric a subject of academic study; Nobel Laureate in Literature 2016
biography: Bob Dylan was born Robert Allen Zimmerman in Duluth, Minnesota, on 24 May 1941 and grew up in Hibbing, on the Mesabi Iron Range; he took the name Dylan in 1962, the year his first album appeared. He moved to New York in January 1961, played the folk clubs of Greenwich Village, and released The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan (1963), which made him the leading songwriter of the American folk revival with 'Blowin' in the Wind' and 'A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall'. Another Side of Bob Dylan (1964) began the turn away from protest, and Bringing It All Back Home (March 1965) split its sides between acoustic and electric music; the single 'Like a Rolling Stone' (July 1965) and the album Highway 61 Revisited followed, and the electric set at the Newport Folk Festival in July 1965 became the symbolic break between folk and rock. Blonde on Blonde (1966), John Wesley Harding (1967), Nashville Skyline (1969), Blood on the Tracks (1975), Desire (1976), Infidels (1983), Oh Mercy (1989), Time Out of Mind (1997), 'Love and Theft' (2001), Modern Times (2006), Tempest (2012) and Rough and Rowdy Ways (2020) followed across six decades. His prose includes Tarantula (1971) and the memoir Chronicles: Volume One (2004). He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016 'for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition', the first such prize for a songwriter, and delivered his Nobel lecture in 2017.
literary_profile: Studio albums: Bob Dylan (1962), The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan (1963), The Times They Are a-Changin' (1964), Another Side of Bob Dylan (1964), Bringing It All Back Home (1965), Highway 61 Revisited (1965), Blonde on Blonde (1966), John Wesley Harding (1967), Nashville Skyline (1969), Self Portrait (1970), New Morning (1970), Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid (1973), Dylan (1973), Planet Waves (1974), Blood on the Tracks (1975), The Basement Tapes (1975), Desire (1976), Street-Legal (1978), Slow Train Coming (1979), Saved (1980), Shot of Love (1981), Infidels (1983), Empire Burlesque (1985), Knocked Out Loaded (1986), Down in the Groove (1988), Oh Mercy (1989), Under the Red Sky (1990), Good as I Been to You (1992), World Gone Wrong (1993), Time Out of Mind (1997), 'Love and Theft' (2001), Modern Times (2006), Together Through Life (2009), Christmas in the Heart (2009), Tempest (2012), Shadows in the Night (2015), Fallen Angels (2016), Triplicate (2017), Rough and Rowdy Ways (2020) and Shadow Kingdom (2023). Books: Tarantula (1971), Writings and Drawings (1973), Lyrics 1962-1985 (1985), Chronicles: Volume One (2004), The Philosophy of Modern Song (2022).
stylistic_characteristics: Long, accumulating stanzas built from short end-stopped phrases; surreal and collaged imagery drawn from the newspaper, the Bible, the blues and the folk song; a voice pitched between the preacher and the street hustler; refrain and repetition used as musical rather than logical structure; and a habit of addressing a 'you' whose identity shifts within the song.
intellectual_concerns: The individual against a society that has made a fool of him; the mutability of fortune; love and its betrayals; the American past and its myths, from the Civil War to the Depression; the prophetic and the biblical; and, after 1979, an explicit religious vocabulary that has divided his critics ever since.
historical_significance: Dylan's Nobel Prize in 2016 settled, at least officially, a question the academy had argued for fifty years: whether the song lyric belongs to literature. The award cited 'new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition', and the two songs the Norton Anthology of American Literature prints - 'Like a Rolling Stone' and 'It's Alright, Ma (I'm Only Bleeding)' - are the pair on which that claim most often rests, both from 1965, the year he moved from acoustic protest to electric poetry.
bibliographical_notes: The albums and books above come from Wikipedia's article on Dylan, checked against album discographies and the Nobel citation; they were not checked against a printed bibliography, and the many singles, outtakes, live releases and Bootleg Series volumes are not listed. Installment 10 records two Norton selections, both songs from 1965; every other song and album has no record, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, short-story writer and essayist of Acoma Pueblo writing in English
literary_identity: Acoma Pueblo poet and storyteller, a central figure of the Native American Renaissance, whose sequence-poems of journey, rain and continuance made the oral tradition of his people a form of American poetry
biography: Simon Joseph Ortiz was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico, on 27 May 1941 and was raised in the Acoma Pueblo village of McCarty, in an Acoma-speaking family; his father was a stonemason, carpenter and woodcarver, and Ortiz has described how the older people's stories and songs formed his sense of language. He was educated at Fort Lewis College and the University of New Mexico, where he took an MFA in 1981, and worked in various jobs before teaching. His first chapbook, Naked in the Wind, appeared in 1971; a long manuscript was then divided into Going for the Rain (Harper & Row, 1976) and A Good Journey (Turtle Island Foundation, 1977), the two books that made him, with Leslie Marmon Silko and James Welch, one of the founders of the Native American Renaissance. Fight Back: For the Sake of the People, for the Sake of the Land (1980) turned to the uranium belt of New Mexico and the tercentenary of the Pueblo Revolt; From Sand Creek (1981) is his best-known single book, a sequence on the 1864 massacre of Cheyenne and Arapaho people and on the condition of the Native American veteran. Woven Stone (1992) collected the three earlier books with a long preface, and After and Before the Lightning (1994) followed a winter on the Rosebud Sioux reservation. He has taught at the University of New Mexico, the University of Toronto and Arizona State University, edited the journal Puerto del Sol, and served as lieutenant governor of the Pueblo of Acoma.
literary_profile: Poetry: Naked in the Wind (1971), Going for the Rain (1976), A Good Journey (1977), Fight Back: For the Sake of the People, for the Sake of the Land (1980), From Sand Creek (1981), Woven Stone (1992, collecting the three previous books), After and Before the Lightning (1994) and Out There Somewhere (2002). Prose: Song, Poetry and Language (1977), A Poem Is a Journey (1982), the stories in Men on the Moon (1999) and the essay collections Speaking for the Generations (1998) and The Good Rainbow Road (2002).
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, spoken line, often very short, with almost no punctuation; repetition and refrain carried over from song and prayer; narrative sequences rather than single lyrics, organised as journeys; direct address to a child, a listener or a place; and a vocabulary that keeps Acoma words and place-names untranslated.
intellectual_concerns: Journey and return, and the land as a source of identity; rain, drought and the shiwana, the rainmakers of Pueblo religion; fatherhood and the teaching of children; the survival of the Pueblo peoples since the Spanish conquest; the uranium mines and the exploitation of Indian labour; the massacres of the nineteenth century, especially Sand Creek; and language itself as the means by which a people continues.
historical_significance: Ortiz is one of the three or four writers by whom the Native American Renaissance is dated, and the Norton Anthology of American Literature prints five of his poems, of which three fall inside the period. His insistence that the poem is a form of continuance rather than a private artefact - 'the only way to continue is to tell a story' - made him the theorist as well as the practitioner of a literature written for a community, and his influence runs through the Native writing of the following decades.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia, the Poetry Foundation and Gale author pages and a survey of his career at nativeamericanlit.com, checked against the contents of Woven Stone (1992); they were not checked against a printed bibliography, and the essays, chapbooks and edited volumes are not all listed. Installment 10 records three Norton selections - 'Earth and Rain, the Plants & Sun', 'Passing through Little Rock' and the excerpt from From Sand Creek - so the other collections, the stories and the essays have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.
